title: On-Call Schedule Software for Residencies, Done for You
description: Operate on-call scheduling software yourself, or have the schedule built for you? What QGenda, Amion and a managed service each actually do for a residency.
content:
Summary

  • Self-service scheduling software helps, but someone in the program still enters the rules, runs the build and checks it for ACGME problems, usually the chief resident.
  • The core decision for programs is not which software to use, but whether to operate a tool yourself or receive a finished schedule built to the rules.
  • With any tool the program runs itself, there is still the "annual knowledge reset," where scheduling know-how leaves each year with the outgoing chief.
  • A managed service like Scheduling Wizard solves these problems by delivering a finished schedule built to the requirements that apply, taking the operator burden off the program.

You finally convinced your department to move away from the spreadsheet. You picked a scheduling platform, sat through the demo, got the login credentials, and then... realized someone still has to learn the rules.

Someone still has to input every ACGME duty hour rule, every vacation request, every night float rotation, every PTO conflict. Someone still has to manually check if the auto-generated schedule actually violates anything before it goes out.

That someone is usually the chief resident, who is also trying to become a physician.

For most programs, a scheduling platform moves the work rather than removing it.

Instead of wrestling with a spreadsheet, you're wrestling with a platform. Knowing the rules, entering them correctly and catching the violations still falls to whoever runs the tool.

There's also a structural problem that no amount of software features can fully fix: the annual knowledge reset. Every year, a new chief resident takes over.

The outgoing chief spent 12 months mastering your program's unique scheduling logic: which rotations conflict, which attendings have protected days, which residents need accommodation. When they graduate, that knowledge walks out the door.

The incoming chief starts from scratch, makes the same early mistakes, and the cycle repeats. A new tool does not change that; the next chief still has to learn it from zero.

So the question to start with is not "which scheduling software should we use?" but this one:

Do you want to operate scheduling software yourself, or do you want a finished schedule built to your rules delivered to you?

Those are two different products.

Here is a breakdown of both approaches.

Path 1: Self-Service Residency Scheduling Software

This path makes sense for programs with dedicated administrative staff who are comfortable living inside a scheduling platform, or for those who genuinely want granular, hands-on control over every scheduling decision.

If that's you, here are the most common self-service tools and what you need to know about each:

QGenda

A platform built for health systems, and highly customizable. Your team sets up the rules and builds or generates the schedule in it, so the setup and the review stay with you. It tends to suit Graduate Medical Education (GME) offices with dedicated scheduling staff better than a chief resident fitting it around clinical work.

Amion

One of the best-known names in residency scheduling, built primarily for publishing and viewing a schedule.

One user in r/managers wrote that Amion "is not fully meeting the needs of the team, especially regarding automation." Many programs use it to publish a schedule that was built elsewhere. It is familiar to most residents, and it is built for publishing a schedule rather than building one.

In short, these tools are useful if you have the time, technical comfort and dedicated staff to run them well. For a chief resident doing this on top of a full clinical load, the build is still theirs to do, just inside a platform.

Path 2: Managed Residency Scheduling Services

This path is for chief residents and program directors who are done treating scheduling as a software problem and want a finished schedule instead. You don't want to learn another tool. You want a finished, fair schedule built to the rules, and you want someone else to produce it.

This is the managed service model, and it works differently from anything in the self-service category:

  1. You submit your rules: ACGME duty hour rules, rotation requirements, resident vacation requests, clinic commitments, attending preferences, fairness goals, and any program-specific policies.
  2. Our team builds a complete, finished schedule: built to all of your rules at once, rather than flagging the ones a draft broke.
  3. You receive a finished schedule, as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you, ready for whatever platform you publish through.

You do not have to run a scheduling platform. The schedule comes to you, and where it goes from there is up to you.

Here is our entry in this category:

Scheduling Wizard

Scheduling Wizard is a Y Combinator (YC)-backed managed scheduling service (W26) purpose-built for medical residency and fellowship programs. It delivers complete block, clinic, call and attending schedules, and it operates as a fully done-for-you service.

Programs send their rules and receive finished schedules built to the ACGME requirements they tell us apply, as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you. There is no software to learn or platform to configure, and the review at the end is a check rather than a repair job.

What makes Scheduling Wizard different:

  • The ACGME requirements you tell us apply go in while the schedule is built, alongside your own rules, with the Common Program Requirements as the floor; the review at the end is a check, not a repair job.
  • Subspecialty-specific rules are built into the schedule itself. This is the first question on most of our sales calls, and the answer is that you tell us which requirements apply, and they go into the build rather than being left to an operator to configure.

Solves the Annual Knowledge-Loss Problem

The written rule set for your program lives with the Scheduling Wizard team, not with the current chief resident. When a new chief rotates in, the institutional knowledge doesn't reset; it transfers without interruption.

Works Alongside Existing Tools

Which platform you use is entirely up to you. Many programs upload our schedules into the platform they already have, others use the live view we build, or both.

  • Fairness is built into the schedule. Night shifts, weekend call and holiday coverage are balanced across the cohort as evenly as your rules allow, and the tallies come back with the schedule so anyone can check them.

Scheduling Wizard currently serves 20+ hospitals and practices and 30+ departments, and builds for fellowships, provider groups and private practices as well.

What Changes When the Build Is Handed Over

The Rules Go In During the Build

With a self-service tool, the checking usually happens once your team has built the schedule. With a managed service, the rules are applied while the schedule is built, starting from the ACGME requirements you tell us apply.

Fairness You Can Count

When a schedule is built by hand under time pressure, the tallies drift, and residents notice. Threads on unequal night shifts are full of residents who are sure they drew the short straw and have no numbers either way. It hurts morale, and over a year it adds to burnout.

The July Problem, Handled

In a managed service model, your rule set doesn't live inside a chief resident's head. It lives with the service provider. When July arrives, the new chief reviews and approves rather than rebuilding from scratch. The institutional continuity that took years to develop doesn't evaporate with each graduating class.

Operate a Tool, or Receive a Schedule

The best residency scheduling software for your program is whichever one actually produces a schedule you can use, without eating a hundred hours of a chief resident's time or leaving ACGME compliance as a manual checklist item.

If your program has dedicated scheduling staff and wants full hands-on control, self-service tools like QGenda are worth exploring. They're real tools with real capabilities, and for the right team, they work.

But if scheduling takes too long, slips on rules nobody wrote down, looks different every year because the knowledge leaves with each chief, and leaves residents feeling it is unfair, the fix is less about software and more about who does the build. A service takes the build off your plate and delivers a finished schedule built to the rules.

That is what Scheduling Wizard does.

Where we fit

Scheduling Wizard builds physician schedules as a service. We do this full time. You send us your rules and requests, the written ones and the local ones that are harder to put on paper, and we send back the finished schedules in the format your program wants, as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you.

Major redrafts are part of it. When someone goes on leave, a rotation changes or coverage shifts mid-year, we rebuild around it rather than handing you a correction exercise. For the specifics, see our page on residency call scheduling.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a managed scheduling service?

A managed scheduling service builds and delivers the finished schedule for you, built to your rules, so you never operate any software yourself. There is no platform to learn. You send us your program's rules, like ACGME rules, vacation requests and fairness goals, and receive a finished schedule, typically as a spreadsheet, ready for distribution.

How does Scheduling Wizard handle the ACGME rules for my specific subspecialty?

You tell us which requirements apply to your program, the Common Program Requirements and anything your specialty's Review Committee adds, and we write them down with you alongside your own rules before the first build. They go into the schedule while it is built rather than being flagged afterwards. We do not assume we know your requirements better than you do; we ask.

Do I have to stop using Amion or QGenda to use Scheduling Wizard?

No. It is entirely up to you. We build the schedule either way, and deliver it in the format and structure you want: Excel or Google Sheets, or a custom live view we build for you if that is useful. Many programs keep Amion or QGenda for day-to-day viewing and upload our schedules straight into it; others use the live view, or both. Whatever works best for your program.

What is the primary difference between Scheduling Wizard and self-service software?

The primary difference is who does the work. With self-service software, you are responsible for learning the platform, inputting all the rules, building the schedule, and manually checking for violations. With Scheduling Wizard, a managed service, we do all of that for you. You provide the rules, and we deliver a finished schedule built to the requirements. That takes the administrative burden off the program and ends the annual knowledge loss when chief residents graduate.

How are mid-year schedule changes handled?

For changes that reshape the block, a leave, a rotation change, a coverage gap, you tell us and we rebuild the rest of the block to the same rules. Redrafts through the year are part of the service.

How does a managed service prevent the "annual knowledge reset" when a new chief resident takes over?

A managed service prevents the annual knowledge reset by keeping your program's rule set written down with the service, not in the head of the current chief resident. When a new chief takes over in July, they don't have to start from scratch. All the complex rules, attending preferences, and rotation conflicts are already written down. The handoff is simple, and the usual early-year mistakes are much less likely.

What kind of schedules can Scheduling Wizard create?

Scheduling Wizard can create a wide range of complex medical schedules, including annual Block schedules, monthly or quarterly Call schedules, and resident Clinic schedules. The service is also used to build schedules for fellows and attending physicians, accommodating the unique rules of each role.
